Europe Romania Shoots Down Drone That Breached Its Airspace Two Romanian Air Force F-16 aircraft and two Italian Air Force Eurofighter Typhoon aircraft were scrambled to monitor the drone incursion. Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print A Romanian F-16 fighter jet shot down a drone that breached Romania's airspace on July 24. U.S. Air Force/Senior Airman Christopher Campbell Timothy Frudd 7/24/2026 | Updated: 7/24/2026 0:00 X 1 A Romanian F-16 fighter jet shot down a drone that breached the country’s airspace on July 24, marking the first time Romania has done so despite dozens of previous airspace incursions. The Romanian Defense Ministry said its radar surveillance system “detected an aerial target” on Friday morning about 12 miles east of Sulina, a town in Tulcea County, Northern Dobruja, Romania. It said the target, which was later identified as a drone, penetrated the country’s airspace. The drone incursion follows a series of violations of Romanian airspace, including a drone crash in May that left two people injured in an apartment building. There have been repeated breaches of airspace on NATO’s eastern flank during the war between Russia and Ukraine. In response to Friday’s drone incursion, two Romanian Air Force F-16 aircraft assigned to the 86th Air Base and two Italian Air Force Eurofighter Typhoon aircraft, deployed to the 57th Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base, were scrambled to monitor the situation. The two Italian fighter jets had been on NATO Air Policing duty prior to the incident, according to the defense ministry. The Romanian Defense Ministry confirmed that one of the F-16 fighter jets engaged the drone with an air-to-air missile and shot it down over an unpopulated area near Padina, Buzau County. Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Toiu said Friday was the first time a drone had been intercepted and destroyed in Romanian airspace. Related Stories Allies to Reinforce Air Defenses Along NATO Eastern Flank After Russian Drone Incident, Says Romania Day in Photos: Russian Drone Explodes in Romania, Bogota Metro Test Run, and Israeli Strike in Lebanon “This morning, around 11:00 a.m., a Romanian pilot in an F-16 aircraft shot down a drone that had entered our country’s airspace,” Romanian President Nicusor Dan said in a statement posted on X on July 24. “The area was uninhabited, so the pilot was able to fire without any risk involved. Currently, teams from institutions with relevant responsibilities are investigating the area to provide all the details about the incident.” Toiu credited the successful downing of the drone to the dedication of the F-16 pilot, the quick response of the Romanian military, and close coordination with the Italian Eurofighter aircraft. “This multinational combined effort underlines how NATO is ready and able to react to any potential air threats, 24/7, to safeguard our territory and protect our people,” NATO’s Allied Air Command said in a statement following the incident on July 24. The command said an investigation was launched after the drone was shot down. It also noted that the downing of the drone came as Romania, NATO, and other nations had been actively obtaining ground-based interceptors to strengthen defense capabilities. In a statement on social media, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Friday’s drone incursion marked another violation of the eastern part of European airspace. “I commend the Romanian military for their swift and effective response, safeguarding our shared security,” she said. “Strengthening defence and deterrence along our Eastern border remains a top priority.” Gen. Gheorghita Vlad, the Romanian army’s chief of staff, said on Friday that Romania had not yet identified the origin and purpose of the drone. He indicated that the drone appeared to be a recognized type of attack drone but said it was too soon to form conclusions. “Visually, the pilots reported the drone looked to be a Shahed type,” he said. The Shahed attack drones, which were designed by Iran, have been repeatedly used by Russia during its war with Ukraine. In May, the Romanian Defense Ministry said a Russian drone entered Romania’s airspace and crashed into an apartment building. Two people were injured in the drone crash. The defense ministry said the incident occurred while Russia was launching drone attacks on infrastructure and civilian targets in Ukraine near the Romanian border. In June, the Romanian government confirmed that its allies were prepared to help the country reinforce air defenses along the eastern flank of NATO. Toiu said the Russian drone incursion in May accelerated efforts to strengthen the country’s defenses. “Our top priority is to ​increase capabilities,” Toiu said. She added, “There is a common understanding that we need to strengthen the eastern flank, not just in Romania. This is a conversation we’re having with the Baltics and all countries on the eastern flank.” The leaders of NATO’s eastern member nations issued a joint statement in May highlighting the need to consolidate NATO’s air defenses against airspace violations. “Repeated airspace violations on the Eastern Flank underscore the urgent need to continue strengthening NATO’s air and missile defence, including against [unmanned aircraft system] threats,” the leaders said. Reuters contributed to this report. Share this article Mark Us Preferred on Google Share this article Leave a comment Timothy Frudd Author Timothy Frudd is a reporter for The Epoch Times. https://www.dw.com/en/tunisia-s-human-ri.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JrLK Tunisians have been protesting against President Kais Saied this summer, demanding the restoration of democracy and calling for the release of jailed activists and journalists amid a worsening economic and social crisis Image: Jihed Abidellaoui/REUTERS Advertisement "Most civil society organizations are in a state of shock today," Messaoud Romdhani, a Tunisian human rights activist told DW. "Those who criticize the authorities or situation in Tunisia face widespread repression," he explained, adding that "most have been accused of money laundering, which leads to the suspension of their activities." Another Tunisian activist, who spoke with DW on condition of anonymity, also said that increasingly people were thinking twice before speaking in public or even choosing to work on sensitive issues. "What worries me most is the chilling effect: When organizations face suspension and activists face prosecution or detention , the uncertainty itself becomes a form of pressure," he said. Human Rights Watch has also raised the alarm. In its latest report , published Wednesday morning, the international rights watchdog concludes that Saied is attempting to shutter Tunisia's civil society entirely. "It is clear that the authorities are abusing every tool at their disposal to close the space for civil society in Tunisia," the report reads. The watchdog also points out that civil society groups in Tunisia have played a key role in holding power to account, delivering essential services and advocating for people's human rights . "The government has used abusive, arbitrary prosecutions, detentions, financial investigations and suspension of organizations in an attempt to stifle these voices," Bassam Khawaja, a deputy director in the Middle East and North Africa Division at Human Rights Watch and editor of the report, told DW. He added that it was clear the idea was to shut down all opposition and independent voices in the country. "This amounts to a total crackdown on civil society in Tunisia," he said. Young Tunisians are increasingly unhappy with the government, while older Tunisians are more satisfied that a decade ago, according to one survey Image: Jihed Abidellaoui/REUTERS Saied was elected president democratically in 2019. But in July 2021, he dissolved parliament and launched a power grab. Since then, he has dismantled most democratic bodies, repressed political dissent and arrested opposition figures . For Anthony Dworkin, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations who focuses on human rights and democracy, Saied's goals remain unchanged. "They have been the same for the last five years, namely to consolidate power and remove potential checks on and critics of his rule," he told DW. Saied has rejected accusations that he is an authoritarian ruler and argued that his measures are necessary to tackle corruption and uphold democracy. He has accused critics of receiving foreign funding to stir unrest and undermine Tunisia's national interests . DW reached out to the Tunisian presidency for comment but had not received a response by the time of publication. Growing discontent prompts calls for Saied's resignation Despite the widespread crackdown on dissent, some people still dare criticize the government. On July 25, the fifth anniversary of the president's power grab, thousands took to the streets of the capital, Tunis, to protest worsening living conditions, democratic backsliding and the government's handling of basic services. The demonstrations came amid widespread water and electricity outages, which Saied has described as "premeditated acts aimed at inflaming the situation by all means and spreading lies and rumors to sow confusion." In late August, protesters once again called on the president to step down by chanting "The people want the fall of the regime," a popular slogan from the 2010-2011 Arab Spring uprising . The demonstration was initiated by Nafas, a new citizen-led umbrella initiative that was launched in May. Mohamed Hawel, a university teacher and member of the Nafas collective, told the news agency AP that Nafas was created to unite people around basic necessities, including water, electricity and food. Growing gap between older, younger Tunisians Despite some unity at these protests, according to an Arab Barometer survey there is an emerging generational divide in Tunisia. A report published in July on the basis of a survey conducted in the fall of 2025 found that older and less educated people had vastly different views on the country's economic and political conditions from younger, better educated people. The survey showed that the older generation saw the current political and economic situation in the most positive light since the Arab Spring and had more trust in the government than over the past decade. In comparison, younger Tunisians were more pessimistic about the country's economic and political development. They also remained more skeptical of state institutions while maintaining a high trust in civil society organizations: 49% of people between the ages of 18-39 expressed trust in these, compared with only 32% of those aged 40 and older. "What really stands out in Tunisia is that the recent decline in trust in civil society is almost entirely a story about older Tunisians. Two years prior, there was almost no generational gap between citizens," Michael Robbins, the director of Arab Barometer, told DW. "Since then, trust in civil society among Tunisians 40 and older has fallen quite sharply, while it has not changed meaningfully among those who are aged 18-39." Tunisia has a population of approximately 12 million people. People aged 18–39 account for roughly 30% of the population, while those aged 40 and older account for approximately 43%. "I think the notion of a divided society is overstated," said Dworkin. "Moreover, the recent demonstrations are not large enough to pose a serious threat to Kais Saied," he added, while admitting that Saied had lost considerable public support over his failure to improve the country's economy. "But there are no attractive political alternatives and people are also tired of political upheaval." In his view, many Tunisians are just trying to get by with daily life, while many others are looking to emigrate. DW's Tarek Guizani in Tunis contributed to this report. Lucia Tallová’s “Moving Clouds” in Berlin Slovak visual artist Lucia Tallová is presenting an extensive solo exhibition at Berlin’s Palais Populaire. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3kg.text: Image source, Tennessee Department of Corrections By Ione Wells ,Â Reporting from North America correspondent in Nashville Â and Â Sareen Habeshian Published 2 October 2026, 20:20 BST Updated 1 hour ago Warning: This article contains details that readers may find distressing Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike was unconscious, intubated and on a ventilator on Thursday night, after authorities failed to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyers say in court filings. Pike, 50, was injected with two lethal doses of pentobarbital on Wednesday but remained alive. She was then sent to hospital in an ambulance. Pike remained critically ill and was being treated at a Nashville-area hospital. Lawyers for Pike, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer, are seeking to have her sentence commuted after the failed execution attempt. Pike's lawyers filed an emergency motion on Friday to preserve "any and all evidence" related to her botched execution. Hospital staff are working to save her life and clear the drug used, pentobarbital, from her system, the filing states. During the execution attempt, prison officials tried to start intravenous (IV) lines by using at least seven needles on Pike, according to her lawyers. At one point, Pike herself offered guidance of where they could try. "One needle was bent in a 90-degree angle when it was removed," the filing states. While receiving the two doses, "she could be heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly throughout the procedure", her lawyers said. Tennessee Governor Bill Lee ordered an independent review into Pike's botched execution and he halted all executions in the state for the year. The state's department of correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out". Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have not not offered any explanations about what went wrong. What happened in the failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next? Published 4 hours ago I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's Published 7 hours ago Pike's attorneys previously warned that her conditions, including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins meant there was a risk she would experience "unnecessary" pain and suffering during a lethal injection. In the latest filings, her lawyers allege that "at no point did any member of the execution team realise that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms Pike's body". They are requesting that all relevant physical, written and electronic evidence is preserved. Dr Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike's defence team, said two doses of pentobarbital was enough that "she would have surely died" had it entered her bloodstream in normal circulation. The only possible explanation for her survival, Zivot said, "is that the pentobarbital blood level was never high enough to cause death" and that blisters on her arm after the botched execution indicated a ruptured vein. So, instead of entering Pike's bloodstream, he said, the pentobarbital was more likely to have spread across the tissue under her skin. Pike's medical condition of thrombocytosis may have also played a role, forming blood clots at the injection site that would potentially block pentobarbital from entering her veins. Regarding the possibility the pentobarbital was degraded, Zivot explained that if this was the case, it could be due to factors including poor manufacturing or improper storage. Image source, Family handout Image caption, Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed in the 1995 murder The attempted execution went ahead after multiple failed, last-minute legal challenges by Pike's lawyers. The US Supreme Court thwarted two separate efforts to stop the lethal injection. Tennessee's governor also denied a clemency request from Pike, the only woman on the state's death row. Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer in 1995. She was sentenced to death the following year after a media frenzy around the killing in Knoxville, Tennessee. Before the killing, Pike had accused Slemmer of insulting her and trying to steal her then-boyfriend. Pike's boyfriend and co-defendant Shipp was 17 at the time so was spared the death penalty under state law. He was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole and remains in prison. Photograph: Matsadaash/AP Egypt Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detained Calls for release of six Matsadaash staff after one is charged, while whereabouts of other five remain unknown William Christou in Jerusalem Sun 4 Oct 2026 11.16 EDT First published on Sun 4 Oct 2026 11.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days after an entire newsroom was detained in what rights groups have said is a crackdown on press freedoms. Last week, authorities arrested six journalists from the independent fact-checking and investigative platform Matsadaash – literally meaning “don’t believe” – accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and publishing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood . The outlet’s six journalists, Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal, were arrested by security forces over the course of two days. On Sunday, Egyptian authorities charged Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading false news, according to a statement by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, a NGO. The charges came after an interrogation that lasted from 10pm to 8am and focused exclusively on material published by Matsadaash, the rights group said. Ashraf was to be held for 15 days, pending investigation, while the whereabouts of the other five journalists were still unknown. View image in fullscreen Egyptian authorities have charged the journalist Mohamed Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading fake news. Photograph: Matsadaash/AP Abdelrahman Mansour, the co-founder of the platform, denied having any association with the Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational movement that was designated a terrorist organisation by Egypt in 2013 after the former president Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, was ousted in a coup. Mansour called the arrests “one of the gravest attacks on journalism in Egypt’s modern history”. “My colleagues were doing what journalists should do: asking difficult questions, uncovering facts, and reporting on issues that affect people’s lives. They deserve recognition for their work. Instead, their homes were raided, and all six were taken away,” he said. “The government must answer this question: why have you arrested six journalists? What have they done beyond doing their jobs?” The Guardian contacted the Egyptian State Information Service for a comment but did not receive a reply by the time of publishing. Dozens of journalists staged a sit-in outside the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate (EJS) in Cairo on Saturday, demanding the release of the Matsadaash staff. Members said they would keep the sit-in open ended until the journalists were released, and the EJS said it would convene an emergency meeting on Monday. The EJS had filed a request with the ministry of interior and public prosecutor for the release of the journalists, as well as for information on their whereabouts. More than 80 rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, condemned the arrests as a violation of freedoms, and demanded the immediate release of the Matsadaash staff. The arrests came little over a week after the US government waived its human rights conditions on $320m (£242m) in military aid to Egypt, citing Cairo’s “helpful role” to US national security after the US-Iran war. The US gives about $1.3bn in aid to Egypt annually, but a portion is contingent upon the Egyptian government meeting certain human rights and democracy-related requirements. The US has withheld portions of aid several times since the 2013 coup owing to Egypt’s poor human rights record, but has largely kept funds flowing. This year, Washington waived the human rights requirement in total, as doing so was “essential for the US-Egypt relationship and US national security priorities”, according to a state department memo revealed by Reuters. While saying that he was unsure whether the arrests were linked to the recent waiver, Mansour said: “The use of the national security waiver on human rights conditions by the US by many years, a willingness by other states to look the other way on Egypt’s human rights record … certainly enables violations like this to occur more easily.” Cairo has for years faced criticism for its human rights abuses, with the rights monitor Freedom House saying Egyptian security forces “engage in human rights abuses and extrajudicial killing with impunity”. Since the Egyptian president Abdel Fatah al-Sisi took power in the coup that ousted Morsi, civil liberties have been curbed and domestic political opposition has been violently crushed. Egypt ranks 169th out of 180 countries on the Reporters Without Borders Press freedom index. Freedom of the press is tightly restricted in the country and independent platforms such as Matsadaash are rare. About 26 journalists are held in Egyptian prisons, according to the EJS.
